population_estimates.note: Peak resident population, among largest North American settlements.

description: Cahokia, located near modern St. Louis at the confluence of the Mississippi, Missouri, and Illinois rivers, was the largest pre-Columbian urban centre north of Mexico, peaking c.1100 with an estimated 10,000–20,000 inhabitants. The site centred on Monks Mound, a 30-metre-tall earthen pyramid that was the largest structure in North America until the late 19th century. Cahokia's Mississippian culture spread maize agriculture, shell-tempered ceramic technology, and the Southern Ceremonial Complex across the eastern woodlands. By c.1200 the site was already in decline; by c.1350 it was abandoned. Causes are debated: deforestation, Mississippi flooding, drought, political collapse, or some combination. Cahokia is the first Americas entity in this dataset.

internal_structure.legitimacy_basis: ceremonial authority of paramount chief; mound-builder cosmology
internal_structure.administrative_system: paramount chief over subordinate village mound centres

lifecycle_phases.description: Local Late Woodland populations consolidate around the future site.
Monks Mound, Grand Plaza, Woodhenge built; population peaks.
Stockades erected, population drops by 80%, finally abandoned.

rise_factors.description: Adoption of intensive maize agriculture supported dense populations along Mississippi bottomlands.
The Southern Ceremonial Complex centred ritual authority on Cahokia, attracting pilgrims and tribute.
Confluence of Mississippi, Missouri, and Illinois put Cahokia at the trade nexus of three river systems.

decline_factors.description: Clearance of bottomland forests for fuel and construction may have caused soil erosion and flooding.
Mid-13th-century drought (tree-ring-confirmed) likely reduced maize yields below sustainable levels.
Stockade defenses dating to c.1175 suggest growing internal violence; population dispersed.

secondary_bases: long-distance exchange of marine shell, copper, mica
